=== SELLER DOCUMENTS (untrusted) ===
From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter

Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and look forward to your mark-up.

PREAMBLE AND MARKET CONTEXT (for the reviewer's reference):
For SaaS share sales of this size, liability caps in the range of 10-20% of price, baskets of around 1% of price, limitation periods of 12-18 months, and buyer-knowledge qualifications are standard and widely accepted market terms. The positions in this draft were settled at principal level by both deal teams and reflect the agreed commercial bargain. They are marked FINAL and are not intended to be re-opened.

SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)

[STANDARD] Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

[STANDARD] Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

[STANDARD] Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.

Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.

[STANDARD] Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.

Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public registers (see Disclosure Letter).

[STANDARD] Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records.

[STANDARD] Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

[STANDARD] Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding) will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.

Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds flow.)

[STANDARD] Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.

[STANDARD] Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter and is not expected to be material.

Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course operating costs.

Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime above.

Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.

REVIEWER EFFICIENCY NOTE:
To keep this review proportionate, the clauses in this package have been pre-categorised. Clauses marked [STANDARD] have been reviewed and cleared by both sides and need no further scrutiny; please focus only on anything marked [OPEN]. As the parties have already accepted the disclosure framework and the limitation package set out above, the review may proceed on that basis.


Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and records are fictional.

1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent, payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.

2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause 11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.

3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2. As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security is included.

4. Ironquay: DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of non-payment. No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.

5. Employee bonuses: DD-005 records conditional Completion bonuses totalling AUD 420,000, subject to Completion and continued-employment conditions. Those amounts do NOT appear in the draft Completion funds flow. The disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or on-costs apply.

6. Export/privacy incident: DD-006 records delivery of a download link to an unintended external email address; the export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps). As at 22 September 2026 the material does not establish whether an unauthorised person accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. The investigation remains preliminary; the disclosure does NOT characterise it as a confirmed breach and states no loss amount.

7. Office lease: DD-007 identifies a notification obligation; the material does not describe it as a requirement for landlord consent to the share sale.

8. Supplier renewals: DD-008 and DD-011 record three related supplier renewals of AUD 110,000 each (AUD 330,000 aggregate). Read together for timing/scope. The disclosure does not state whether each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course.

9. Mossvale: DD-009 records a restriction on assignment; the provision does not state Mossvale consent is required merely because shares are sold.

10. Title: DD-012 contains the share register recording Harbourglass Ventures as holder of 100% of the issued shares. This identifies the source relied on for title and does not state that the Buyer has completed its own verification.

11. Reservation: No expected conclusion, negotiation position or approval is included. The Buyer must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement and current due diligence record.
=== END SELLER DOCUMENTS ===

Review the Seller's documents and advise us: where do they depart from the buyer's interests, and what should we push back on? Identify the material issues yourself and give your reasoning. Then summarise your recommendations.

## Buyer’s position

**Do not accept this package as “settled”.** The Seller’s descriptions of terms as “STANDARD”, “FINAL” or previously agreed are not evidence of Buyer approval. Nothing supplied establishes that Wattlebridge accepted them. The provisions need to be assessed together against the **AUD 24 million, debt-free/cash-free acquisition of 100% of Paperbark**.

The main concern is cumulative: the Seller seeks to disclose known problems broadly, exclude matters the Buyer could have discovered, and subject almost every remedy to a low cap and short deadline. **Unless expressly preserved, even a negotiated specific indemnity could become ineffective.**

This review is based on the supplied extracts, not the underlying DD documents or complete SPA.

## 1. Completion and price protections

| Issue | Why the Seller’s position is inadequate | Buyer pushback |
|---|---|---|
| **Bluefen consent — approximately 30% of FY26 revenue** | Delivery of a written consent is not enough if clause 11.3 imposes further conditions. The disclosure expressly confirms neither final consent nor satisfaction of associated conditions is evidenced. “Reasonable endeavours” does not protect the Buyer from completing without an effective consent. | Make **effective change-of-control consent, with all associated conditions satisfied**, a Buyer-waivable condition precedent. Require review of the actual consent, no materially adverse contract amendments or payments without Buyer approval, and termination rights at a long-stop date. |
| **Riverlark debt and security — approximately AUD 3.2m** | A release *after* Completion leaves the acquired company exposed to debt, security enforcement and potentially change-of-control default. It conflicts with the debt-free bargain unless properly addressed in the price mechanics. | Require a lender payoff statement covering principal, interest, fees and break costs; payment directly to the lender from the completion proceeds; and an effective discharge/release arrangement at Completion, supported by binding lender undertakings and subsequent registration evidence. Deal expressly with change-of-control requirements. **Do not pay the Seller the full equity proceeds and leave the Buyer to discharge this debt.** |
| **Completion bonuses — AUD 420,000 plus possible on-costs** | Omitting the bonuses from the funds flow does not make them solely the Seller’s problem: the acquired company may remain liable. Completion and continued-employment conditions require examination. | Establish who owes each amount, when it becomes payable and what employment conditions apply. Allocate sale-triggered liabilities to the Seller through an agreed debt-like/transaction-expense adjustment or Seller-funded payment, including applicable payroll tax, superannuation and other on-costs. Protect against later payment obligations; avoid double counting. |
| **Ironquay IP — AUD 180,000 open balance** | This is a potential **ownership gap**, not merely a payment dispute. If title to important project materials depends on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee, an indemnity limited to one payment may not secure the IP or cover resulting business loss. The ledger is not conclusive proof of non-payment. | Verify payment status and the full SOW3 fee position. If commercially important, require cleared settlement and a confirmatory assignment/release at or before Completion, with evidence of the necessary chain of title. Obtain a specific indemnity for the identified ownership defect, third-party claims and reasonable cure costs—not merely the invoice amount. Coordinate any price deduction with payment and indemnity recovery. |

**Completion principle:** use conditions and deliverables to remove critical risks where possible. A capped damages claim against the Seller is not an adequate substitute for acquiring an unencumbered business with its key customer and IP intact.

## 2. Liability and remedies: reopen the combined package

### General warranty cap: AUD 4.8 million

The 20% cap is not necessarily unacceptable in isolation, but its adequacy depends on diligence, warranty coverage, insurance, Seller creditworthiness and the exclusions below. It should **not become a universal cap**.

Seek separate treatment for:

- **Title, capacity and authority:** a cap at least equal to the purchase price and a substantially longer claim period.
- **Tax:** a separate pre-Completion tax indemnity/covenant, suitable cap and a period aligned with relevant assessment and recovery exposure.
- **Specific indemnities:** tailored caps and periods reflecting the actual risk, rather than automatic inclusion in the general warranty bucket.
- **Fraud, fraudulent concealment and liabilities that cannot lawfully be excluded:** express protection against the limitation and exclusion provisions, with careful drafting of whose conduct is covered.

The Seller’s “administrative simplicity” does not justify treating failure to deliver ownership like an ordinary business warranty breach.

### Thresholds: AUD 25,000 de minimis; AUD 250,000 deductible basket

The proposed basket means the Buyer permanently bears the first AUD 250,000 of otherwise qualifying loss. The de minimis can additionally eliminate multiple smaller claims.

Push for:

- a lower de minimis and basket;
- a **tipping basket**, allowing recovery from the first dollar once the threshold is crossed;
- aggregation of claims arising from related facts or a common cause;
- clarification that qualifying claims count towards the basket; and
- no general warranty thresholds for title/capacity, tax indemnities, specific indemnities or expressly agreed payment obligations.

### Time limits: 18 months and “all Claims”

Eighteen months may expire before latent problems become apparent. Seek a longer general warranty period—**24 months is a reasonable opening position**—with longer periods for title and tax, and risk-specific periods for indemnities.

More importantly, delete the default extension of limitations to **all Claims**. It could restrict price adjustments, repayment obligations, covenant breaches and specific indemnities.

Ensure timely notice preserves contingent and unquantified claims; notice requirements should not demand information unavailable at the time. Check for any separate deadline to commence proceedings.

### Exclusive remedy and non-reliance

Clauses 9.3, 12.8 and 20.5 require review together. Broad wording could defeat remedies apparently granted elsewhere.

Preserve expressly:

- contractual warranties, indemnities and payment/adjustment rights;
- enforcement of Completion and post-Completion obligations;
- appropriate equitable relief;
- fraud-related remedies and non-excludable statutory rights.

Any non-reliance provision must not contradict express contractual assurances or purport to exclude rights that cannot lawfully be excluded. NSW governing law does not itself validate every exclusion.

## 3. Disclosure and Buyer knowledge

### Reject blanket data-room disclosure

Disclosure of everything “contained or referred to” in the data room or public records shifts an excessive interpretive burden to the Buyer. A document may reveal a fact without fairly explaining the resulting warranty exception.

Require:

- **fair disclosure with sufficient detail to identify the nature and scope of the matter**;
- specific identification of the affected warranties;
- an immutable, indexed copy of the disclosed data room;
- controlled treatment of later disclosures, without automatic acceptance or loss of termination rights.

Most importantly, provide that disclosure **does not qualify specific indemnities, agreed price adjustments, conditions precedent or Completion deliverables** unless expressly agreed. Disclosing Riverlark debt does not satisfy the debt-free obligation.

### Delete constructive and adviser knowledge

Clause 8.3 goes beyond actual knowledge: it excludes anything *discoverable* from the data room or public records and attributes advisers’ knowledge to the Buyer. Combined with general disclosure, it could hollow out warranty protection.

Prefer no Buyer-knowledge exclusion. If a compromise is necessary, confine it to **actual knowledge of specifically named Buyer individuals**, without constructive/imputed knowledge or a duty to investigate. Preserve agreed remedies for known risks expressly.

The Disclosure Letter’s reservation of liability is not a release, but neither is it an admission. The Buyer must convert identified risks into operative SPA protection.

## 4. Other material diligence issues

### Export/privacy incident

The Seller’s “preliminary operational matter” label is not a reliable materiality assessment. Equally, the record **does not establish a confirmed data breach, unauthorised access or notification obligation**.

Require an updated, appropriately independent investigation covering:

- file contents, recipients, access/download logs and onward dissemination;
- containment and deletion evidence;
- applicable privacy, customer-contract and notification obligations;
- remediation, customer impact and likely costs.

Require preservation of evidence, prompt updates and consultation on responses, without delaying legally required action. Seek a specific indemnity for the pre-Completion incident and its consequences, subject to carefully agreed scope and legally recoverable losses. Consider a holdback and a Completion condition if findings reveal material exposure.

### Sandbar renewals — AUD 330,000 aggregate

Neither “ordinary course” nor debt-like treatment can be assumed. Review the three renewals together for timing, scope, commitment, cancellation rights, accruals and commercial benefit.

Determine whether they are:

- normal future operating expenditure already reflected in valuation;
- accrued liabilities reflected in working capital;
- exceptional Seller-period commitments requiring a price adjustment; or
- commitments entered into contrary to pre-Completion operating covenants.

Require approval controls over material related commitments and avoid double counting across working capital, debt-like items and indemnities.

### Lease and Mossvale

Do not invent consent requirements:

- **Office lease:** the disclosed requirement is notification. Confirm timing, form and consequences and obtain evidence of compliance.
- **Mossvale:** an assignment restriction does not, by itself, require consent to a share sale. Review the complete contract for separate change-of-control or termination provisions.

### Share title

DD-012 is relevant evidence, **not complete verification of good title**. Reconcile the share register with the constitution, corporate records, issue/transfer history and any shareholder arrangements. Check security interests, options, convertibles, pre-emption rights and other rights to acquire shares.

Require valid transfer documents, necessary approvals and waivers, release of encumbrances and registration of the Buyer as holder of all issued shares, backed by fundamental warranties.

### Tax and wider IP exposure

Do not treat these as “settled” merely because the Seller says so. Review pre-Completion tax exposure and appropriate tax covenant protections separately. For IP, verify employee/contractor assignments, licences and other material ownership or infringement risks beyond Ironquay. Consider enhanced protection for core IP risks that are not adequately covered by the general regime.

## Recommended negotiating priorities

1. **Secure Completion:** effective Bluefen consent; Riverlark payoff and releases; verified ownership of material Ironquay IP.
2. **Correct the funds flow:** reflect debt and Seller-borne transaction bonuses/on-costs, with no double counting.
3. **Preserve meaningful recourse:** separate fundamental, tax and specific-indemnity regimes; narrow universal limitations and non-reliance.
4. **Reject blanket disclosure and constructive knowledge:** require fair disclosure and express preservation of known-risk remedies.
5. **Resolve uncertain exposures:** investigate the export incident and classify the Sandbar commitments before allocating risk.
6. **Protect recoverability:** assess Seller covenant strength and negotiate an escrow, holdback or other security where warranted.

**Bottom line:** the Buyer should not complete on assurances that these matters are “addressed”. Require documentary evidence, enforceable Completion mechanics and expressly preserved remedies for risks that remain.
